the_rotation_constraint_is_unsatisfiable.the_proof: THOSE FOUR ROWS BETWEEN THEM USE SEVENTEEN OF THE TWENTY-FIVE ORDERED ADJACENT PAIRS FIVE BANDS CAN FORM. THE EIGHT THEY NEVER USE ARE KK, LL, NN, TT, UU, LN, NL, NT AND TN, WHICH IS NINE, AND EVERY ONE OF THOSE NINE IS A PAIR OF THE SAME BAND OR A PAIR AMONG THE THREE WOMEN'S BANDS. THE LOCK-UP BAND AND THE UNIT BAND MAY THEREFORE BE FOLLOWED BY THEMSELVES AND BY NOTHING ELSE, SO IN ANY ROW THAT SHARES NO ADJACENT PAIR WITH THOSE FOUR THE TWO LOCK-UP CHAPTERS MUST STAND TOGETHER AND THE TWO UNIT CHAPTERS MUST STAND TOGETHER, AND BOTH PAIRS MUST SIT AT ONE END OF THE ROW, WHICH A ROW OF TEN CANNOT DO TWICE OVER. A SOLVER OVER EVERY LEGAL ROW RETURNS ZERO. THE CONSTRAINT WAS SATISFIABLE ONCE, AT 0074, AGAINST THREE ROWS, AND IT IS NOT SATISFIABLE NOW AGAINST FOUR.
the_rotation_constraint_is_unsatisfiable.what_was_done: THE MINIMUM OVERLAP BETWEEN A LEGAL ROW AND THE FOUR PRIOR ROWS WAS COMPUTED OVER ALL 113400 LEGAL ROWS, EACH BAND EXACTLY TWICE AND NO THREE IN A ROW. THE MINIMUM IS TWO SHARED ADJACENT PAIRS, AND EVERY ROW THAT REACHES TWO PUTS TWO BANDS SIDE BY SIDE TWICE, WHICH IS A WORSE SHAPE THAN SHARING THREE PAIRS AND SHARING NONE OF THEM BY ACCIDENT. THE ROW TAKEN IS THE BEST-SHAPED ROW AT THREE SHARED PAIRS, AND THE THREE ARE NAMED: THE LOCK-UP INTO THE TEN, THE TWELVE INTO THE UNIT, AND THE UNIT INTO THE LOCK-UP. **THE RULE IS RECORDED AS BROKEN HERE AND NOT SATISFIED BY A FIGURE, BECAUSE A FIGURE PRINTED UNDER A CLAIM THAT IT COULD NOT BE IS THE FAULT THIS ACCOUNT KEEPS RECORDING.** A HUMAN MAY RULE THE ROW RULE AND TAKE THIS UP; A WRITER MAY NOT.

cards.0935: At number twelve a woman of seventy-eight has a square socket cut into the stone plinth of the back wall, once bedded round an iron pipe in lead, and means to put the hand into it with the fingers together and turn the hand a quarter on its own axis inside it, to find out how far the socket goes and what stands in the floor of it. Nothing cut, nothing levered, no lead taken out, no room entered.
cards.0936: At the unit a man in his early forties has a length of scaffold tube standing on end in the corner of the yard with something wedged across its bore, and means to press the four fingers of one hand down into that bore while the thumb lies across the rim outside, to find out how far the tube is hollow and what is across the far end of it. Nothing lifted, nothing shaken out, no tube picked up, no room entered.
cards.0937: At the lock-up a woman in her late forties has a roller shutter in the bay with one slat lying over the slat below it, and means to put two fingers of one hand flat into that lap with the other two bent back out of it, to find out how deep the lap runs and what lies in the step of it. Nothing lifted, no shutter raised, no slat bent, no room entered.
cards.0938: At number ten a woman in her early thirties has the back of the house boarded with weatherboards that lie one over another, and means to push the hand into the step between two of them with the fingers bent at the first joint, to find out how far the step runs and what stands at the far end of it. No board taken off, no nail touched, no line put right, no room entered.
cards.0939: At number nine a woman in her late fifties, alone in the house, has a cast airbrick set in the boundary wall, and means to push the hand in behind it through its open face with the fingers spread and the thumb outside along the near edge, to find out how deep the space behind it goes and what closes it. Nothing unscrewed, no vent taken out, no wall opened, no room entered.
cards.0940: At number ten a woman in her early thirties has a wooden sill laid over the flags at the back door, and means to lay the hand flat and push it under that sill with the palm down and the fingertips leading, to find out how far the sill stands off the flags and what lies under its nose. Nothing lifted, no sill taken up, no door moved, no room entered.
cards.0941: At number nine a woman in her late fifties, alone in the house, has a concrete path that has sunk and opened a line against the kerb, and means to push the hand down into that line with the thumb laid along the near edge, to find out how deep it goes and what is in the bottom of it. Nothing taken up, no kerb lifted, no joint filled, no room entered.
cards.0942: At number twelve a woman of seventy-eight has a zinc lining at the foot of the chimney stack where the metal is turned up the face of the pot and folded back on itself, and means to put the fingers bent at the first joint into that fold with the knuckles held outside it, to find out how far the fold carries the hand and what stands at the end of it. Nothing lifted, no pot touched, no flue entered, no room entered.
cards.0943: At the unit a man in his early forties has two trestles leaning against the office wall of the yard with a wedge standing between them, and means to put the hand into that wedge with the four fingers spread wide on the far face and the thumb laid along the near one, to find out how deep the wedge goes and what is against the wall at the back of it. Nothing moved, no trestle taken down, no wall opened, no room entered.
cards.0944: At the lock-up a woman in her late forties has a corrugated sheet on the office wall that has lifted off its bottom fixing and stands away from the wall along one line, and means to put the closed fingers of one hand into that gap and rock the hand twice against the wall behind it, to find out how far the gap runs and what stands against the wall along it. Nothing unscrewed, no sheet taken down, no packing put in, no room entered.

EVERY ONE WAS BROUGHT UP WITH REAL MATERIAL AND NOT WITH FILLER: how a bolster opens a square socket and why downwards is the wrong way to cut one, what a lead caulk does as it shrinks, the pipe's own round kept in a ring of lead after the pipe is cut out, why a rolled-and-welded tube leaves a lump in its own bore, why a tube out of true holds its water in a line along itself, how a corner is the only place on a yard where nothing can be knocked over, how a lap in a shutter slat is pressed in the mill and not made, why a slat that cannot move slides and one that can scrapes, why the crease in the middle of a bay shuts tighter than the ends, that boards are sawn to a pattern and not to a width, why a taper at the head of a board keeps its step, why one board of a run is held on one stud and lifts at its end, that an airbrick is a two-part box and not a plate with a slot, why a fitter always leaves the cavity behind a vent clear, and why a hood over a vent keeps what comes in, why an elm sill is sawn and not planed and what a sawn surface collects, why a bed is laid fat in the middle and drawn off at the ends, that wood is far harder across a grain than anybody expects, that three nail holes in a flag under a sill date a winter and nothing else on that wall does, why a river sand has no edges to lock with, that a granite kerb does the sideways work on a path of flags on edge, that a hard grey flag of another make shuts a line at its own width, why sheet metal is a poor material for a fold and a good one for a channel, what a hammered edge in soft sheet loses in twenty years, why a pointer has to stop at a sheet metal edge, why two trestles leaning on a wall cannot be tied or wedged and can only be stable because the ground under their feet is level, and why a fourth timber nailed across a trestle top is a thing nobody does and everybody does after the second time they have carried it.
